parts.label: c
parts.key: Only the C–Br bond is broken and a C–O bond made (the C–H, C–C and O–H bonds cancel). ΔH = broken − formed = 285 − 358 = −73 kJ mol−1. A positive answer earns 1 mark.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: d.i
parts.key: Break 1½ O=O + 4 C–H + Cl–Cl = 1½(498) + 4(414) + 242 = 2645 kJ mol−1. Form C=O + 2 C–O + 2 O–H + 2 H–Cl = 804 + 2(358) + 2(463) + 2(431) = 3308 kJ mol−1. ΔH = 2645 − 3308 = −663 kJ mol−1. Counting every bond on both sides (6649 − 7312) gives the same result. +663 earns 2 of 3.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: d.ii
parts.key: Any one: bond enthalpies are averages taken over many compounds, so they are not specific to these molecules; bond enthalpies apply to gases, but this reaction involves liquids; enthalpies of formation are measured for the actual substances, so that value is more specific.

parts.label: d.iii
parts.key: Use ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants): −4 = ΔHf(ester) + (−286) − [(−278) + (−484)]. Rearranging gives ΔHf(ethyl ethanoate) = −480 kJ mol−1. The first mark is for the correct expression; +480 earns 1.

parts.label: b
parts.key: Draw two humps that start at the same reactant level and finish at the same, higher product level (endothermic). Label ΔH as an upward arrow from reactants to products. Label Ea from reactants to the top of each hump, with the catalysed hump lower. Marks: both curves sharing start and end points, ΔH labelled as endothermic, both Ea labelled. Arrows pointing down for Ea or ΔH lose the mark.

parts.label: b.i
parts.key: Break C=C (614) + H–Br (366) = 980 kJ mol−1. Form C–C (346) + C–H (414) + C–Br (285) = 1045 kJ mol−1. ΔH = 980 − 1045 = −65 kJ mol−1. Including all the C–H bonds gives the same result. +65 earns 1 mark.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: b.ii
parts.key: Any two: bond enthalpies are average values; enthalpies of formation are specific to the actual compounds; bond enthalpies apply to gases, but the product here is a liquid; bond enthalpy calculations ignore the change of state.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.key: Take three values from the data booklet: Br–Br bond enthalpy 193, first IE of Ca 590, and electron affinity of Br −325 (×2 = −650 kJ mol−1). Going round the Born–Haber cycle: 648 + 178 + 31 + 193 + 590 + 1145 = ΔHlatt + 650, so ΔHlatt = +2135 ≈ +2100 kJ mol−1. Lattice enthalpy is positive in the IB convention (breaking the lattice), so −2100 earns 2 of 3.
given: 1st ionization energy of Ca = 590 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; electron affinity of Br = −325 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: b.iii
parts.key: Endothermic. Heating turns the mixture blue, so the equilibrium shifts right toward CoCl42−. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: b.iv
parts.key: Draw an endothermic profile, with products above reactants (consistent with b.iii), and label reactants and products. Show E<sub>a</sub> as an arrow from the reactant level up to the peak, and ΔH as an arrow from the reactant level to the product level.

parts.label: c.i
parts.key: Fill the boxes in order up the cycle. Bottom-left box (species): Ca(s) and Cl2(g), the elements in their standard states. Process box: first and second ionization energies of Ca, taking Ca(g) to Ca2+(g). Right-hand box (species after electron affinity): Ca2+(g) and 2Cl−(g), the gaseous ions that form the lattice.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.key: Ca2+ has a larger ionic radius than Mg2+ (same charge), so the distance between ion centres is greater, the electrostatic attraction is weaker and the lattice enthalpy is lower. The answer must refer to ions, not atoms.

parts.label: f.i
parts.key: Using only the bonds that change: break C=C (614) + O–H (463) = 1077 kJ; form C–C (346) + C–O (358) + C–H (414) = 1118 kJ. ΔH = 1077 − 1118 = −41 kJ. Counting every bond gives 3196 − 3237, the same −41 kJ. A positive sign only earns 2 of 3 marks.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: f.ii
parts.key: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −235 − [(+52) + (−242)] = −45 kJ. Here +52 is for ethene and −242 for steam (gaseous water). +45 earns 1 mark.

parts.label: f.iii
parts.key: Bond enthalpies are average values across many compounds, so they differ slightly from the actual bond strengths in ethene and ethanol. Enthalpies of formation are specific to each compound.

parts.label: b.vi
parts.key: KOH is in excess, so HCN limits: n = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol. Heat released = 0.00200 × 13 300 J = 26.6 J. The total volume is 50.0 cm3 ≈ 50.0 g of solution, so ΔT = 26.6 ÷ (50.0 × 4.18) = 0.127 K (°C).
given: c = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>; q = mcΔT
assume density 1.00 g cm<sup>−3</sup> and c of water

parts.label: a.iii
parts.key: Break C≡O (1077) + Cl–Cl (242) = 1319 kJ mol−1. Form C=O (804) + 2 × C–Cl (2 × 324) = 1452 kJ mol−1. ΔH = 1319 − 1452 = −133 kJ mol−1. Note CO has a triple bond, so use the C≡O value.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: a.iv
parts.key: Show reactants higher than products (exothermic, matching the −133 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> from the previous part), with a hump between them. Label “Reactants”, “Products” and ΔH as a downward arrow from the reactant level to the product level.

parts.label: a.i
parts.key: Build a Hess cycle through the combustion products: ΔH = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products). Reactants: −1301 + 2(−286) = −1873 kJ mol−1. Product: C2H6 = −1561. ΔH = −1873 − (−1561) = −312 kJ mol−1. Note the order is the reverse of the formation-data rule.

parts.label: b.ii
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: c
parts.key: Moles of ethanol = 4.00 ÷ 46.08 = 0.0868 mol. Heat released = 0.0868 × 1367 kJ (ΔHc from section 14) = 119 kJ = 119 000 J. ΔT = q ÷ mc = 119 000 ÷ (500.0 × 4.18) = 56.9 K (56.8 accepted). 500.0 cm3 of water is taken as 500.0 g. Using your bond-enthalpy value from (b)(ii) is also accepted, giving ΔT ≈ 52.5 K.
given: c = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>; q = mcΔT

parts.label: e.i
parts.key: ΔHf(H2O(l)) = −285.8 kJ mol−1 from section 13; K and H2 are elements (zero). For the equation as written: ΔH = 2(−481.8) − 2(−285.8) = −392.0 kJ. Per mole of potassium, halve it: −196.0 kJ mol−1.

parts.label: d.i
parts.key: Label the x-axis reaction progress / reaction coordinate (not “time”) and the y-axis potential energy / enthalpy. Draw an exothermic curve: products below reactants. Show Ea as an upward arrow from the reactant level to the peak. Three marks: axes, exothermic shape, Ea.

parts.label: b.v
parts.key: CO is less stable than CO2. On the enthalpy profile CO (+ ½O2) sits higher, and converting it to CO2 is exothermic, releasing energy. The lower-enthalpy species is the more stable one.

parts.label: a.i
given: c = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>; q = mcΔT

parts.label: a.ii
parts.key: Add the percentage uncertainties. Mass: 0.02 ÷ 400.00 × 100 = 0.005%. ΔT is the difference of two readings at ±0.5 °C each, so ±1.0 °C on 21.0 °C = 4.76%. Total ≈ 4.77% (4.76% accepted if only the temperature is counted).

parts.label: a.iii
parts.key: Repeat the experiment and take an average. Also accepted: use more water, run the experiment longer for a larger ΔT, or name a more precise instrument (digital thermometer or temperature probe, more precise balance). “More precise equipment” without naming it, or references to accuracy, score nothing.

parts.label: b.i
parts.key: M(propan-1-ol) = 60.11 g mol−1. Mass burned = 20.00 − 18.20 = 1.80 g, so n = 1.80 ÷ 60.11 = 0.0299 mol. ΔHc = −35 100 J ÷ 0.0299 mol ≈ −1200 kJ mol−1 (negative, because combustion is exothermic). One assumption, e.g.: all heat goes to the water / no heat loss, the gel is pure propan-1-ol, complete combustion, or the copper absorbs no heat.
given: C 12.01, H 1.01, O 16.00, so M(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH) = 60.11 g mol<sup>−1</sup>

parts.label: b.ii
parts.key: Percentage error = |experimental − literature| ÷ literature × 100 = (2021 − 1200) ÷ 2021 × 100 ≈ 40.6%, using ΔHc = −2021 kJ mol−1 from section 14. Ignore the signs.

parts.label: b.iii
parts.key: Heat loss to the surroundings, together with a way to reduce it: insulate the calorimeter, shield it from draughts, move the flame closer, or use a closed (food) calorimeter. A coffee-cup calorimeter or “add a lid” is not accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.key: Energy per gram of each fuel = (1 ÷ M) × ΔHc. Propan-1-ol: (1 ÷ 60.11) × 2021 ≈ 33.6 kJ g−1. Ethanol: (1 ÷ 46.08) × 1367 ≈ 29.7 kJ g−1. So the ethanol gel releases less energy per gram. The conclusion only scores when supported by both calculations.

parts.label: b.vi
parts.key: Let x = the C≡O bond enthalpy. ΔH = broken − formed: x + 2(463) − [2(804) + 436] = −41. So x = −41 − 926 + 2044 = 1077 kJ mol−1. A negative bond enthalpy earns 1 mark; bond enthalpies are always positive.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: c.i
parts.key: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = (−87.2) + (−74.0) − (−248) = +86.8 kJ. Here −74.0 is for CH4 and −248 for liquid propanone. The positive sign means the reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.key: Draw an endothermic profile (products higher than reactants), matching +86.8 kJ. Label ΔH as an arrow from the reactant level up to the product level, and E<sub>a</sub> as an arrow from the reactant level to the peak.

parts.label: f
parts.key: Data booklet values: ½ × Br–Br (193) = 96.5, IE of Na = 496, EA of Br = −325 kJ mol−1. Lattice enthalpy = ΔHatom(Na) + ½ΔHvap(Br2) + ½E(Br–Br) + IE(Na) + EA(Br) − ΔHf(NaBr) = 107 + 15 + 96.5 + 496 − 325 + 361.5 = +751 kJ mol−1. Copying the data-booklet value of 754 is not accepted.
given: 1st ionization energy of Na = 496 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>; electron affinity of Br = −325 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: g
parts.key: ΔHsol = ΔHlattice + ΔHhyd(Na+) + ΔHhyd(Br−) = 751 + (−424) + (−328) = −1 kJ mol−1. The markscheme flags hydration enthalpy as outside the new (2025) syllabus, but the method is a standard Hess cycle.

parts.label: a.i
parts.key: Sum ΔHf of reactants: +88.7 (CS2) + 2(−241.8) (H2O as gas) = −394.9 kJ mol−1. Sum of products: −393.5 (CO2) + 2(−20.6) (H2S) = −434.7 kJ mol−1. ΔH = products − reactants = −39.8 kJ mol−1. The usual slip is using −285.8 for liquid water, which gives +48.2 and earns 1 mark.

parts.label: c.i
parts.key: Break C=O (804) + H–H (436) = 1240 kJ; form C–H (414) + C–O (358) + O–H (463) = 1235 kJ. ΔH = broken − formed = +5 kJ mol−1. Breaking every bond in CO2 and remaking one C=O gives the same answer (2044 − 2039).
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: c.ii
parts.key: Add the absolute uncertainties: 0.1% of each bond enthalpy used is 0.804 + 0.436 + 0.414 + 0.358 + 0.463 = 2.475 kJ. Divide by the answer: 2.475 ÷ 5 × 100 ≈ 50% (or about 80% if you broke and remade all the bonds). Subtracting two large, similar totals leaves a small ΔH with a huge relative uncertainty.

parts.label: c.iii
parts.key: H–H. This bond only occurs in the H2 molecule, so its value is measured for that one molecule and not averaged over many compounds.

parts.label: f.i
parts.key: Draw two humps that start at the same reactant level and finish at the same, higher product level (endothermic). Label ΔH as an upward arrow from reactants to products. Label Ea from reactants to the top of each hump, with the catalysed hump lower. Marks: both curves sharing start and end points, ΔH labelled as endothermic, both Ea labelled. Arrows pointing down for Ea or ΔH lose the mark.

parts.label: b.i
parts.key: Break N≡N (945) + 3 H–H (3 × 436 = 1308) = 2253 kJ. Form 6 N–H (6 × 391) = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ. A positive sign earns 2 of 3.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: b.ii
parts.key: The N–H bond enthalpy is an average value from many compounds and may not match the actual N–H bond in NH3. ΔHf data are specific to NH3, so they are more accurate.

parts.label: b.iii
parts.key: The graph shows the percentage of ammonia falling as temperature rises. ΔH is negative, so the forward reaction is exothermic. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, shifting the equilibrium left and lowering the yield.

parts.label: f.i
parts.key: Only one C–H and the Cl–Cl break: 414 + 242 = 656 kJ. Form C–Cl + H–Cl: 324 + 431 = 755 kJ. ΔH = 656 − 755 = −99 kJ. Counting all four C–H bonds gives 1898 − 1997, the same result. +99 earns 2 of 3.
given: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, data booklet section 12)

parts.label: f.ii
parts.key: Draw the reactant line (CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub>) above the product line (CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl), since the reaction is exothermic. Add an arrow from reactants down to products labelled ΔH = −99 kJ. A labelled E<sub>a</sub> hump is an accepted alternative for the second mark.

parts.label: a
parts.key: q = mcΔT = 20.0 g × 4.18 J g−1 °C−1 × 57.3 °C ≈ 4790 J = 4.79 kJ. ΔHc = −q ÷ n = −4.79 ÷ (8.75 × 10−4) = −5470 kJ mol−1 (−5470 to −5480 accepted). The negative sign is needed because combustion releases heat.
given: c = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>; q = mcΔT

parts.label: c.i
parts.key: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −398.9 − (−306.4 + 0) = −92.5 kJ mol−1. Cl2 is an element in its standard state, so its ΔHf is zero.

parts.label: c
parts.key: Rearrange q = mcΔT: c = q ÷ (mΔT) = 1000 J ÷ (50 g × 44.4 K) = 0.45 J g−1 K−1. Convert 1 kJ to 1000 J first; a change of 44.4 °C equals a change of 44.4 K.

parts.label: b.i
parts.key: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = [(−635) + (−393.5)] − (−1207) = +179 kJ, using the data table for CaO, CO2 and CaCO3. Decomposition is endothermic; −179 earns 1 mark.

parts.label: b.iv
parts.key: Draw an endothermic profile: products (CaO + CO2) above reactants (CaCO3), consistent with +179 kJ. Label the x-axis reaction progress / reaction coordinate (not “time”) and the y-axis potential energy / enthalpy. Mark Ea from the reactant level to the peak.

parts.label: b.v
parts.key: ΔH stays the same, because the reactants and products are unchanged. Ea is lower, because the catalyst provides an alternative pathway.

book.label: Practice question 1
book.sol: C. ΔH = +164 kJ mol−1, so the reaction is endothermic. Heat is taken from the surroundings and the temperature decreases. Products have higher enthalpy than reactants, so they are less stable.

book.label: Practice question 2
book.sol:
Energy for a 1 K rise = mass × c.

  1. Water: 1 kg × 4.18 kJ kg−1 K−1 = 4.18 kJ.
  2. Copper: 1000 kg × 0.385 kJ kg−1 K−1 = 385 kJ.

book.label: Practice question 3
book.sol: a. Same q and same m, so c = q ÷ (mΔT) is inversely proportional to ΔT. X warms by half as much as Y (5 °C against 10 °C), so c(X) is twice c(Y).

book.label: Practice question 4
book.sol:
a. Water has the larger specific heat capacity (4.18 against 2.44), so more heat is needed to warm 50 g of it by 50 °C.

  • b is false: ethanol has the lower c, so it warms more.
  • c is false: water gains what ethanol loses, 4.18(T − 20) = 2.44(50 − T), so T ≈ 31 °C, not 35 °C.
  • d is false: cooling by the same amount, water releases more heat because its c is larger.

book.label: Practice questions 5 and 6
book.sol:
5. q = mcΔT = 30 g × 4.18 J g−1 K−1 × 30 K = 3762 J ≈ 3.76 kJ.

6. ΔT = q ÷ (mc) = 675 J ÷ (0.125 kg × 385 J kg−1 K−1) = 14.0 K. Convert kJ to J and g to kg so the units match.

book.label: Question 1 · Topic review
book.sol: A model answer: if the temperature of the surroundings (usually water) rises, heat has left the system and the change is exothermic (ΔH < 0); if it falls, the change is endothermic (ΔH > 0). Measuring ΔT with a known mass of water lets you calculate the heat transferred, q = mcΔT, and from the moles of the limiting reactant the enthalpy change, ΔH = −q ÷ n. The sign also tells you the relative stability of reactants and products: in an exothermic change the products are lower in energy and more stable. Measured values are usually less exothermic than accepted values because of heat loss.

book.label: Question 2
book.sol: D. ΔH is negative, so the reaction is exothermic. The products are lower in energy, so the reactants are less stable than the products.

book.label: Question 3
book.sol:
D. In an endothermic reaction the products sit above the reactants, so the climb from reactants to the peak (forward Ea) is larger than the climb from products to the peak (reverse Ea).

  • A is wrong: exothermic products have less energy.
  • B is wrong: for an exothermic reaction the forward Ea is smaller.
  • C is wrong: endothermic products are less stable.

book.label: Question 4
book.sol: A. 26.6 kJ is released when 2 mol of Fe form (ΔH is negative, so energy is released). Per mole of Fe: 26.6 ÷ 2 = 13.3 kJ released.

book.label: Question 5
book.sol: B. Reactants lower in energy than products means an endothermic change. HBr(g) → H(g) + Br(g) only breaks a bond, and bond breaking always absorbs energy. A (combustion), C (forming a lattice) and D (neutralization) are all exothermic.

book.label: Question 6
book.sol:
1. Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH: +226 kJ mol−1.
  2. Accepted equations, e.g. 4NO2(g) + O2(g) + 2H2O(l) → 4HNO3(aq), or 2NO2(g) + H2O(l) → HNO3(aq) + HNO2(aq).

book.label: Question 7
book.sol:
1. At about 3 minutes, where the temperature starts to rise (the dashed vertical line).
  2. Y is a reading taken while the reaction is in progress: the mixture is still heating up and has not yet reached its maximum temperature.
  3. About 54 °C, read where the extrapolated cooling line meets the time of mixing (3 min). Assumption: heat is lost at the same constant rate during the reaction as during cooling (or: the reaction is instantaneous).
  4. Zinc should be in excess. The CuSO4 volume and concentration are fixed, so with zinc in excess all the CuSO4 reacts every time. The amount reacting (0.0250 mol) is then known and the same in every trial, and changing the mass of zinc doesn't change it.
  5. The solution has a density of 1.00 g cm−3 (25.00 cm3 = 25.00 g) and the same specific heat capacity as water; the mass and heat capacity of the zinc and beaker are ignored.
  6. The calculated ΔH will be less exothermic (smaller in magnitude) than the theoretical value, because some heat is lost to the surroundings and absorbed by the beaker, even with extrapolation.

book.label: Question 8
book.sol:
1. ΔT = 22.6 − 21.3 = 1.3 °C. q = mcΔT = 7.8 g × 4.18 J g−1 K−1 × 1.3 K = 42.4 J = 0.0424 kJ.
  2. Per gram of chip: 0.0424 kJ ÷ 1.2 g ≈ 0.035 kJ g−1 released, so ΔHc ≈ −0.035 kJ g−1. This is far too small because most of the heat from the flame goes into the air, not the water.

book.label: Practice question 1
book.sol:
ΔH = Σ broken − Σ formed: −185 = [BE(Cl–Cl) + BE(H–H)] − 2 BE(H–Cl) = (242 + 436) − 2x.

2x = 678 + 185 = 863, so BE(H–Cl) = 431.5 kJ mol−1 (data booklet: 431).

book.label: Practice question 2
book.sol:
Broken: 4 C–H + 2 O–H = 4(414) + 2(463) = 2582 kJ mol−1.

Formed: 3 H–H + C≡O = 3(436) + 1077 = 2385 kJ mol−1.

ΔH = 2582 − 2385 = +197 kJ mol−1 (endothermic).

book.label: Practice question 3
book.sol:
1. CH4(g) + Cl2(g) → CH3Cl(g) + HCl(g)
  2. Broken: C–H + Cl–Cl = 414 + 242 = 656. Formed: C–Cl + H–Cl = 324 + 431 = 755. ΔH = 656 − 755 = −99 kJ mol−1.
  3. Exothermic: ΔH is negative because more energy is released forming the new bonds than is absorbed breaking the old ones.
  4. The products are more stable, because they are lower in energy.

book.label: Practice question 4
book.sol:
Build the target from the equations: 2 × eq 2 (2C → 2CO2), 3 × eq 3 (3H2 → 3H2O), and eq 1 reversed (to make ethanol a product).

ΔH = 2(−394) + 3(−286) + (+1367) = −788 − 858 + 1367 = −279 kJ mol−1.

book.label: Practice question 5
book.sol:
Target: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O. In the cycle, go from reactants down to the elements (N2, H2, O2), then up to the products.

  • 4NH3 → 2N2 + 6H2: eq 2 reversed ×2 = +184 kJ
  • 2N2 + 2O2 → 4NO: eq 1 ×2 = +132 kJ
  • 6H2 + 3O2 → 6H2O: eq 3 ×3 = −1716 kJ

ΔH = 184 + 132 − 1716 = −1400 kJ for the equation as written (−350 kJ per mole of NH3).

book.label: Practice question 6
book.sol: The enthalpies of combustion are experimental values with their own uncertainties and are rounded. When several of them are multiplied and combined, those errors add up. Data from different sources or conditions may also not match exactly. The ΔHf in the data booklet was measured independently, so the two values differ slightly.

book.label: Practice question 7
book.sol:
Target: 3C(s) + 3H2(g) + ½O2(g) → CH3COCH3(l). ΔHc values: C −394, H2 −286, propanone −1790 kJ mol−1.

Summation: 3C + 3O2 → 3CO2 (3 × −394 = −1182); 3H2 + 1½O2 → 3H2O (3 × −286 = −858); 3CO2 + 3H2O → CH3COCH3 + 4O2 (reversed, +1790). Total = −250 kJ mol−1.

Cycle: ΔHf = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) = [3(−394) + 3(−286)] − (−1790) = −250 kJ mol−1. The data booklet gives −248.

book.label: Practice question 8
book.sol:
1. H2 is an element in its standard state, so its ΔHf is zero by definition.
  2. ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = [3(0) + (−110.5)] − [(−74.0) + (−241.8)] = +205.3 kJ mol−1. Note that H2O is a gas here.
  3. Bond enthalpies are average values from many compounds, not the actual bonds in CH4, H2O and CO. ΔHf values are specific to each substance.

book.label: Practice question 9
book.sol:
1. Step 2 is the combustion of ethene plus hydrogen: ΔH = ΔHc(C2H4) + ΔHc(H2) = −1411 + (−286) = −1697 kJ mol−1.
  2. Step 3 is the combustion of ethane, −1561 kJ mol−1. By Hess's law, step 1 = step 2 − step 3 = −1697 − (−1561) = −136 kJ mol−1.
  3. Accurate: it uses experimentally measured ΔHc values for these actual substances, not average bond enthalpies. Approximate: the data values carry experimental uncertainty and are rounded, and those errors combine; they apply only under standard conditions.

book.label: Practice question 10
book.sol:
Going round the cycle from the elements to MgO(s) by the long route:

ΔHf = ΔHat(Mg) + IE1 + IE2 + ΔHat(O) + EA1 + EA2 − ΔHlattice

= 148 + 738 + 1451 + 249 + (−141) + 753 − 3791 = −593 kJ mol−1.

The lattice enthalpy is subtracted because the cycle travels against its arrow: forming the lattice from gaseous ions releases 3791 kJ.

book.label: Activity · Combustion equations
book.sol:
1. C8H18(l) + 25/2 O2(g) → 8CO2(g) + 9H2O(l), ΔHc = −5470 kJ mol−1
  2. C6H12O(l) + 17/2 O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l)
  3. CH2O2(l) + ½O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(l), ΔHc ≈ −255 kJ mol−1
  4. C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l), ΔHc = −2803 kJ mol−1
  5. C2H5Cl(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l) + HCl(aq) (the corrosive acid is HCl)

One mole of fuel each time, so fractions of O2 are allowed. Look up the cyclohexanol and chloroethane values in your copy of section 14; I've left them out rather than guess.

book.label: Activity · Formation equations
book.sol:
1. 3C(s) + 4H2(g) → C3H8(g), ΔHf ≈ −105 kJ mol−1
  2. C(s) + 3/2 H2(g) + ½Cl2(g) → CH3Cl(g), ΔHf ≈ −82 kJ mol−1
  3. 2C(s) + 3H2(g) + ½O2(g) → C2H5OH(l), ΔHf ≈ −278 kJ mol−1
  4. 7C(s) + 3H2(g) + O2(g) → C6H5COOH(s), ΔHf ≈ −385 kJ mol−1
  5. C(s) + ½O2(g) → CO(g), ΔHf = −110.5 kJ mol−1
  6. C(s) + 5/2 H2(g) + ½N2(g) → CH3NH2(g), ΔHf ≈ −23 kJ mol−1

Elements always appear in their standard states: C(s, graphite), H2(g), O2(g), N2(g), Cl2(g). Values are rounded standard-table values; check them against your data booklet.

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Data-based question 1
book.sol:
1. The minimum temperature is about 19.5 °C, the steady reading before the zinc is added.
  2. Exothermic. The temperature rises sharply once the reaction starts, so heat is released into the solution.
  3. Heat is lost to the surroundings while the reaction is going on, so the highest temperature actually recorded (about 59 °C) is too low. Extrapolating the cooling line back to the moment of mixing (t = 2.5 min) estimates the temperature that would have been reached with no heat loss (64.0 °C), giving ΔT = 64.0 − 19.5 = 44.5 °C.
  4. To find Q you need the mass (volume) of the solution heated and its specific heat capacity (assume water, 4.18 J g−1 K−1). To find ΔH you need the amounts of reactants (mass of zinc, concentration and volume of CuSO4) to work out which is limiting and its moles; then ΔH = −Q ÷ n.

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Data-based question 2
book.sol:
1. Plot temperature (y) against volume of NaOH (x). The points rise steeply to about 20–25 cm3, then fall slowly.
  2. Draw a best-fit line through the rising points (0–20 cm3): T ≈ 22.4 + 0.15V. Draw one through the falling points (30–50 cm3): T ≈ 26.1 − 0.02V. They cross at V ≈ 21.9 cm3 and Tmax ≈ 25.7 °C.
  3. At the crossing point the acid is exactly neutralized. n(NaOH) = 0.600 × 0.0219 = 0.0131 mol = n(HCl). [HCl] = 0.0131 ÷ 0.02500 ≈ 0.525 mol dm−3.
  4. ΔT = 25.7 − 22.4 = 3.3 °C. Total volume = 25.0 + 21.9 = 46.9 cm3 ≈ 46.9 g. q = 46.9 × 4.18 × 3.3 ≈ 643 J. ΔH = −q ÷ n(H2O) = −0.643 kJ ÷ 0.0131 mol ≈ −49 kJ mol−1. This is less exothermic than the accepted −57 kJ mol−1 because of heat loss.

Your graph readings may differ slightly, so answers near these values are fine.

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Practice question 51
book.sol:
1. Systematic: heat is always lost, so ΔT is always too low.
  2. Systematic: a miscalibrated instrument shifts every reading the same way.
  3. Systematic: reading from below the meniscus always gives readings that are off in the same direction.
  4. Random: rounding to the nearest whole number is a limit of the instrument's resolution, and readings are equally likely to be too high or too low.

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Practice question 52

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Practice question 53
book.sol:
1. Student C: |−35 − (−57)| ÷ 57 × 100 = 38.6%. Student D: |−50 − (−57)| ÷ 57 × 100 = 12.3%.
  2. Student C's random uncertainty is small (±4, about 11%), giving a range of −31 to −39 kJ mol−1 that does not include −57. Random error cannot explain the 39% error, so a systematic error (heat loss) dominates. Student D's uncertainty is large (±10, 20%), giving a range of −40 to −60 kJ mol−1 that includes −57. D's result is less precise, but its 12% error can be explained by random error alone.

book.sec: Tools for Chemistry · Data and errors in enthalpy experiments
book.label: Practice question 54
book.sol:
1. Plot ΔHc (y) against number of carbon atoms (x), with vertical error bars of ±40 kJ mol−1 on each point. The points lie close to a straight line sloping downward, becoming more negative by roughly 210 kJ mol−1 per carbon.
  2. Published values (data booklet section 14): methanol −726, ethanol −1367, propan-1-ol −2021, butan-1-ol −2676, pentan-1-ol −3329, hexan-1-ol −3984, heptan-1-ol −4638, octan-1-ol −5294 kJ mol−1. These change by about 650 kJ mol−1 per CH2. The experimental values are only about a third as negative, and the gap grows with chain length. This is a large systematic error: heat lost to the surroundings, and incomplete combustion (soot), always make the values less exothermic.
  3. The points sit close to the line of best fit and the ±40 kJ mol−1 error bars are small compared with the values, so random error has little impact compared with the systematic error.
